stubs.angle: What does setting HttpOnly on an authentication cookie actually protect against?
stubs.answerHinge: HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie and other script access, so an XSS payload cannot read and exfiltrate it, but the browser still sends it with requests, so it does not stop CSRF.

stubs.subtopic: OWASP Top 10: open redirect after login
stubs.angle: Find the line in an ASP.NET Core login action that lets an attacker send users to a phishing site after a successful sign-in (non-runnable ASP.NET Core code).
stubs.answerHinge: Redirect(returnUrl) trusts a user-supplied URL. The fix is LocalRedirect or a Url.IsLocalUrl check, which only accept local paths.

stubs.angle: Which way of rendering a user-provided comment in a Razor view creates a cross-site scripting vulnerability?
stubs.answerHinge: Razor's @ expression HTML-encodes output by default. Html.Raw (or wrapping the input in an HtmlString) skips that encoding and injects user input as markup.

stubs.angle: Why move from role strings in [Authorize(Roles=...)] to named policies, and how do several requirements and several handlers inside one policy combine?
stubs.answerHinge: Every requirement in a policy must succeed (AND). A requirement is satisfied when any of its handlers calls Succeed (OR), unless a handler calls Fail. Named policies keep these rules in one place instead of role names scattered across endpoints.

stubs.angle: Why should an API compare a computed HMAC webhook signature with CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals rather than SequenceEqual or string equality?
stubs.answerHinge: An early-exit comparison returns faster the sooner the bytes differ. That timing leak lets an attacker recover a valid signature byte by byte. FixedTimeEquals takes the same time whichever bytes differ.

stubs.angle: Which measures actually prevent SSRF in a feature that downloads an image from a user-supplied URL?
stubs.answerHinge: Effective measures are a host allowlist, resolving the address and rejecting private, loopback and link-local ranges (checked again on redirects, or with redirects disabled), and network egress restrictions. String blocklists such as "localhost" and CORS do not stop SSRF.

stubs.angle: Which ASP.NET Core error-handling configurations leak internal details to clients in production?
stubs.answerHinge: The developer exception page enabled outside Development, and responses that include exception messages or stack traces, disclose internals. UseExceptionHandler with a generic ProblemDetails response and HSTS do not.

stubs.subtopic: OAuth and OIDC in browser apps
stubs.angle: Why do security guidelines prefer a backend-for-frontend over keeping OAuth access and refresh tokens in localStorage of a SPA, and what new obligations does the BFF bring?
stubs.answerHinge: Any XSS in the SPA can read tokens from browser storage and send them elsewhere. A BFF keeps tokens on the server and gives the browser only an HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie, which in turn makes CSRF protection mandatory.

stubs.angle: A new endpoint shipped without [Authorize] and exposed customer data for a week; as the lead, how do you respond and keep it from happening again across the team?
stubs.answerHinge: Setting AuthorizationOptions.FallbackPolicy to require authenticated users makes every endpoint protected by default, so opening one up needs an explicit, reviewable [AllowAnonymous]. Add tests that enumerate endpoints, rather than relying on reviewers to notice a missing attribute.

stubs.angle: An external penetration test delivers 40 findings a week before launch; how does the lead decide what to fix now, what to accept and who signs off?
stubs.answerHinge: Rank findings by likelihood and impact in your own context, not by the vendor label. Fix exploitable high-risk findings before launch, and record every deferral as an explicit risk acceptance with an owner, a mitigation and a deadline.

stubs.angle: How would you introduce threat modeling into the team's design process so that it finds real issues without becoming a bureaucratic checklist?
stubs.answerHinge: Threat modeling pays off when it runs early on changes that cross a trust boundary. The team walks the data-flow diagram against a structured method such as STRIDE, and every identified threat ends up as a tracked mitigation or an accepted risk.

stubs.angle: For a company with a dozen .NET applications, how do you decide between a managed identity provider, a self-hosted OIDC server and per-application ASP.NET Core Identity?
stubs.answerHinge: The identity provider is security-critical infrastructure that someone must patch, audit and keep available for years. A managed provider moves that burden to the vendor. Self-hosting is justified only by concrete needs such as data residency, offline operation or custom flows, together with a team funded to run it.
